document: OptionPilot Pro — Premium Decay, Moneyness & Intrinsic/Time Value Consolidated Research Report
purpose: Consolidates three research passes from the session into one document: (1) Zerodha Varsity's own teaching on Theta and Moneyness, (2) a concept-by-concept comparison against the OptionPilot Pro codebase as it stands today, and (3) the practical benefits of the Option Composition card built from this research. Every codebase claim was verified by reading server.ts directly, not recalled from memory.

section1_theta.title: What Zerodha Varsity Teaches About Theta (Time Decay)
points: All options lose value as expiration approaches; theta is the rate of that value loss per day, all else held equal.
Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value. All else equal, an option loses some value every day purely because of theta.

Decay is non-linear: early in a series (many days left) an option barely loses value day to day; as expiry nears, decay accelerates sharply. Varsity's own illustration: at 120 days to expiry a premium was around 350, but by 100 days to expiry (just 20 days later) it had only fallen to around 300 — a small move for a large stretch of calendar time.
A short (seller) position benefits from theta — the seller's objective is to hold and pocket premium while it erodes in their favour daily.

For a buyer (this person's actual side), a fresh monthly contract (many days left) is a structurally gentler entry than the last week of the same contract, independent of direction — the mirror image of the seller's early-series advantage.
Indian index options are European-style: a buyer cannot exercise early, only square off before expiry or let it settle at expiry.

section1_1_vega_iv_crush.title: Vega and IV Crush — the Third Source of Premium Loss
points: Vega measures how much a premium moves per 1-point change in implied volatility (IV) — independent of spot movement.
Delta/Gamma affect the INTRINSIC portion of a premium; Theta/Vega affect the EXTRINSIC/time portion — confirmed directly by Varsity's own author.

Around known events (RBI policy, Union Budget, elections, earnings), IV typically rises beforehand and collapses sharply afterward — commonly called 'IV crush.' A premium can fall sharply on IV crush alone, even with a correct directional call.

Practical implication: a drop in a 700–900 premium could be theta (expected), IV crush (event-driven, sudden), intrinsic loss (spot moved against the position), or a mix of all three — and these three look identical on a raw price chart without decomposition.

section2_moneyness.title: What Varsity Teaches About Moneyness (ITM / ATM / OTM)
points: Intrinsic value is the amount a buyer would make exercising the contract right now; it can never be negative.
CE intrinsic value = Spot − Strike. PE intrinsic value = Strike − Spot.
An option carrying intrinsic value is ITM (In the Money); one with none is OTM (Out of the Money); a strike close to spot is ATM (At the Money).
For calls, strikes below ATM are ITM and above are OTM. For puts, it's reversed.
ITM premiums are always higher than OTM premiums for the same underlying/expiry, since ITM carries intrinsic value on top of remaining time value.
For a buyer to have actually gained anything, the option must expire ITM — not ATM, not OTM — confirmed directly by Varsity's author.

section4_implementation.title: What Was Implemented — Option Composition Card (Phase 1)
section4_implementation.note: Built and verified 2026-08-09, following the user-supplied Intrinsic/Time-Value Deep Checklist Research roadmap's Phase 1 scope exactly: observation-only, no change to the deterministic rule-engine score.
details: computeIntrinsicValue(side, spot, strike): CE = max(spot-strike,0), PE = max(strike-spot,0) — pure, stateless, Varsity-grounded formula.
Card shows CE and PE side-by-side for the ATM strike plus its nearest ITM and OTM neighbour on each side.
Each row shows LTP, Intrinsic value (₹ and %), Time Value (₹ and %), and Theta/Vega where available.
Footer text explicitly states the roadmap's own 'do not infer' rule: high intrinsic is not automatically bullish or bearish.
Inserted into the Options tab, directly below the existing Premium Pair card.

practical_benefits.title: Understand what a large premium really means
practical_benefits.description: A ₹700–900 premium now shows exactly how much is intrinsic (real, spot-backed) versus time value (decay-exposed) — directly answering the question that started this research: two contracts with the same price can carry very different risk.

practical_benefits.title: Compare strikes at a glance
practical_benefits.description: Two options at similar premiums can have very different intrinsic/time splits. Seeing the percentage split side-by-side makes it immediate which one is the 'safer' (more intrinsic) versus 'riskier' (more time value) choice before entering.

practical_benefits.title: Existing Greeks get real context
practical_benefits.description: Theta and Vega were already computed but shown as isolated numbers. Displaying them next to the intrinsic/time split gives them meaning — how much of the premium is actually exposed to that decay rate.

practical_benefits.title: The existing verdict system is untouched
practical_benefits.description: This is additional information only. The rule engine's score, verdict, and Haiku's explanation all work exactly as before — nothing here is treated as bullish or bearish by itself, per the roadmap's explicit constraint.
